entry.title: fix: uvicorn was running without --proxy-headers in production
entry.content:
fix: uvicorn was running without --proxy-headers in production

Found by deploying. The api command used a folded ">" scalar:

    command: >
      sh -c "alembic upgrade head &&
             uvicorn ... --port 8000
                     --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips='*' --no-server-header"

A folded scalar collapses newlines only between lines at the same
indentation; a *more indented* line keeps its newline. So sh received three
lines, ran `alembic && uvicorn ... --port 8000`, and then tried to execute
`--proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips='*' --no-server-header` as a command
of its own:

    sh: 3: --proxy-headers: not found

Three consequences, none of which announce themselves:

* uvicorn ran **without --proxy-headers**, so X-Forwarded-Proto from Caddy
  was ignored — the app saw every request as http and every client IP as
  Caddy's container address.
* --no-server-header was dropped too, so the upstream Server header leaked.
* sh exited 127 after uvicorn died, replacing uvicorn's real exit code. The
  container reported "Restarting (127)" no matter what actually went wrong,
  which is how this hid.

One line now, and `exec` so uvicorn replaces sh and receives SIGTERM
directly instead of sh swallowing it and compose waiting out the kill
timeout.

`docker compose config -q` validates this file happily, which is why CI
never saw it — so CI now also rejects any multi-line service command.

27efcf2 staged nihongotutorphase0skeleton.bundle along with its intended
changes — my mistake, a `git add -A` over a working directory that had the
bundle sitting untracked in it. 174 KB of packed git history, checked into
git.

Nothing sensitive: it is this repository's own Phase 0 history, already
public here. But bundles are how work moves between machines, not source,
so *.bundle is ignored now to stop the next one following it in.

The blob stays in history; rewriting main to excise 174 KB is not worth
invalidating every existing clone.

entry.title: plan: reach Claude through Vertex, and STT through Google
entry.content:
plan: reach Claude through Vertex, and STT through Google

Direct Anthropic billing is not available to the owner, and neither is
OpenAI's, so two of the plan's AI decisions were unreachable as written.
Claude now goes through Vertex AI and STT through Google Cloud
Speech-to-Text v2. Both authenticate with the same service account that
already does TTS, so no Anthropic or OpenAI key exists anywhere in the
deployment — one credential, one vendor.

Vertex costs two things, and neither announces itself:

Server-side `fallbacks` is first-party only, so a refusal on Vertex would
have been a dead end. build_async_client registers the SDK's
BetaRefusalFallbackMiddleware instead, which needs an explicit fallback
model because there is no "default" routing policy to defer to. The
first-party path keeps the server-side parameter; sending it to Vertex
would be an error, so the client tracks which route it is on.

The Message Batches API is also unavailable, so offline seed generation
pays full price rather than the 50% batch rate. Recorded in the plan
against the task table that assumed the discount.

STT v2 takes OGG_OPUS natively — no transcode — and its PhraseSet
adaptation replaces OpenAI's `prompt=<target sentence>` trick. 60 min/month
free. openai_api_key is now dead config and is gone rather than left to
invite someone to fill it in.

Class names, the middleware signature, and the batches and fallback
availability were checked against anthropic 1.4.0 as installed, not
recalled.

entry.title: content: put kanji in the examples, and use the plan's field names
entry.content:
content: put kanji in the examples, and use the plan's field names

All 93 example sentences were kana-only while 69 of the 93 headwords carried
kanji. That made example.reading a byte-for-byte copy of example.ja in every
single row, and left the furigana toggle — which the plan turns on by default
from the first vocabulary item — with nothing to render. 89 of the 93 now
carry kanji; the four that do not are the ones whose headword is kana or
katakana.

No new vocabulary enters the sentences: every word was already there in kana,
so this writes the same Japanese properly rather than making it harder. The
examples stay at the `core` stage, where kanji is correct — the kana seeds
are untouched, because the plan's validation gate requires kana-only text
during the bootcamp.

Verified the readings rather than trusting the rewrite: Sudachi reproduces the
pinned reading on 86 of 93 and disagrees on seven — 明日 as あす, 私 as
わたくし, 日本 as にっぽん, 四人 as よんにん, 何時 as なんどき. Each is a real
reading of the characters and the wrong one for this course, which is the
argument for authoring `reading` instead of deriving it. Recorded in
CONTENT.md, since it is the same case the audio section makes.

`source`/`reviewed` were invented names for concepts vocab_lemmas already
defines: now gloss_source ("claude") and gloss_review_status ("needs_review").

Three sentences were duplicated across entries (39/63, 46/68, 13/90, 40/91);
they are distinct now. Four first-person past-tense glosses forced a gender in
Russian — those sentences moved to the present tense, and the remaining
gendered glosses are neutral, since two learners of different genders share
this content.

entry.title: fix: carry the optimiser weights and the budget across as well
entry.content:
fix: carry the optimiser weights and the budget across as well

The learner block claimed to move the learner's settings and moved all but
two of them. daily_budget_usd is cheap to lose — it is one number a learner
can re-enter. fsrs_params is not: it is the personalised FSRS weight vector
the monthly optimiser produces, and the only way to reproduce it is to have
done the reviews again.

Nothing writes fsrs_params yet (Phase 4), which is what made it easy to
miss: a column that is null everywhere transfers correctly by accident, and
the day it stops being null is the day the loss becomes real and silent.
That is the worst possible shape for a bug in a tool whose entire job is not
losing state.

Both read with .get on import, so a payload written before they existed
still applies, and a learner whose optimiser has never run is left alone
rather than having null written over a default.

The round-trip test now sets a 21-float weight vector and asserts it lands.
Dropping the export line again fails it.

entry.title: deploy: size the runbook for the box we actually bought
entry.content:
deploy: size the runbook for the box we actually bought

The prerequisites table said "≥ 2 GB RAM", justified by the ~1 GB idle
footprint. That is the wrong number to check against. deploy.sh runs
`docker compose build` on the server and the Mini App stage runs `npm run
build`, where Vite/esbuild is the memory peak in this stack — so on a 2 GB
CPX12 with no swap it is the build that gets OOM-killed, while the table
says everything is fine.

Split the row into idle and peak, and add a swapfile row before the first
deploy step rather than as troubleshooting: recovering from a killed build
is slower than preventing one. Document building the miniapp image locally
as the fallback if swap is not enough.

PLAN.md still said GCP e2-medium. Hetzner's CX/CAX line has been out of
stock since early September 2026 and GCP lands near $35/mo once the
external IP and balanced PD are counted, so the box is a CPX12. Recorded
with its consequence, and with the one that is easy to miss: off GCP there
is no attached service account, so Phase 2's TTS/STT needs a JSON key on
the box. .env.example said the opposite.

entry.title: deploy: seed content on deploy, and a runbook for the first cutover
entry.content:
deploy: seed content on deploy, and a runbook for the first cutover

deploy.sh ran the migrations and never imported the kana seed, so a fresh
production database would have come up fully migrated with nothing to teach:
the first lesson would have found an empty `kana` table. The import upserts on
natural keys, so running it on every deploy is free and means the server can
never drift from the seed files in git.

docs/DEPLOY.md is the order of operations for the first cutover, host-agnostic
rather than GCP-specific, and covers the three things the README's deploy
section does not.

The webhook is the one that bites: a bot token has exactly one webhook URL, so
production steals it from the development tunnel on boot — and a laptop stack
restarted afterwards steals it back, silently. The runbook says to expect that,
and to take a second token from BotFather for further local work.

Progress transfer needs the timezone fixed *before* the export, because the
payload carries it and the reminder job fires on it.

And DNS has to resolve before the first deploy, not after: Caddy proves domain
control over HTTP, and repeated ACME failures are rate-limited in hours.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: content: core vocabulary tranche 1, and the content/audio contract
entry.content:
content: core vocabulary tranche 1, and the content/audio contract

Ninety-three entries covering what a learner can use in the first sittings
after kana: greetings, people, food, places, time, verbs, adjectives and the
question words. Kanji where that is the ordinary written form, a pure-kana
reading on every entry, no romaji.

Everything ships reviewed=false. The owner reads it before the importer marks
the items active — a learner cannot detect a wrong gloss, she just learns it.

docs/CONTENT.md records why content lives in git rather than in a database,
and settles the audio design: synthesize the reading rather than the written
form, ship MP3 alongside OGG_OPUS so iOS does not fail silently, and address
clips by a hash of (text, voice, rate, encoding) so stale audio cannot
survive an edit. Full coverage measures 4,530 characters — 0.45% of the
monthly free tier, so nothing needs rationing.

entry.title: feat: move a learner's progress between databases
entry.content:
feat: move a learner's progress between databases

Needed to carry existing progress onto a server, and it cannot be a `pg_dump` of the learner
tables. `cards.item_id` points at `items.id`, which is a UUID minted when `import_kana` runs, so
two databases that imported the same seed hold the same 208 syllables under entirely different
ids — verified: あ is `01a07645-e696…` in the dev database and `01a07b8d-a7ac…` in another. Copied
rows would arrive pointing at nothing.

So progress travels keyed by what the content actually is — `(script, char, direction)` — and the
importer resolves that against whatever ids the destination uses. `nihongo-content
export-progress --tg-id N` and `import-progress -i file.json`.

Being re-runnable is the other reason not to use a dump: a learner keeps using the local instance
while a server is being set up, so the export has to be re-applied at cutover against a database
that is already live. Cards match on `(learner, item, direction)`, review logs on
`(card, review_at, rating)`, sessions on `(learner, started_at, kind)`; a second run adds nothing.

What travels: settings, streak, every card with its full FSRS state, every review log, and finished
sessions. What does not: `session_steps` and `daily_plans` are working state for one sitting and are
rebuilt on demand, so an unfinished session is skipped rather than half-copied, and
`ai_usage_ledger` is per-deployment billing rather than learner progress.

A syllable the destination has never heard of is counted and reported, and the CLI exits non-zero —
importing before the seed would otherwise lose progress silently.

Tested by re-minting the content ids underneath an export and checking it still lands: eight tests
covering the id-divergence case, settings and streak, review history, idempotency, the
missing-seed warning and a format-version guard.

entry.title: fix: total orderings, and describe the simulation's variance accurately
entry.content:
fix: total orderings, and describe the simulation's variance accurately

**The ordering bug.** `ORDER BY due` with a LIMIT is not a total order here. A day's cards are
created in one transaction and share an identical `due` — every new production sibling is
`now + 1 day` — so which of them the limit returned was up to Postgres and could differ between two
identical requests. The plan promises that reopening a session replays it, and that promise was only
as good as the physical row order. `id` now breaks the tie in the due and weakest-card queries, and
uuid7 is time-ordered, so the tiebreak also means "oldest first" rather than an arbitrary pick. Same
for the session lookups that resolve with LIMIT 1.

**Correcting an overclaim from the previous commit.** Its comment said seeding the module RNG made
the 30-day run reproducible. It does not. Seeding removes FSRS's interval fuzz as one source, and
this commit removes unstable row order as another, but the step order comes from
`interleave.make_seed(user.id, local_date)` and the learner's UUID is fresh on every run —
deliberately, since each learner is meant to get their own ordering. Different order means different
cards answered at different moments, which feeds back into the schedule.

Measured across four runs after both fixes: streak, completed days and syllables taught come out
identical every time; minutes per day do not. Which is exactly why the assertions are invariants
rather than counts — they hold under any ordering, and pinning the incidentals would only buy a test
that fails for the wrong reason.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: docs: catch the plan and hand-off up with the product
entry.content:
docs: catch the plan and hand-off up with the product

The docs had drifted from the code, which is worse than being out of date: `docs/PLAN.md` still
specified `base = 5` and `min(new + 1, 10)`, so anyone reconciling plan against code would have
"fixed" the code back.

- **PLAN.md** now carries the amended numbers with the measurement as the reason — the sweep that
  showed base 5 leaving a 70%-accuracy learner on 94 of 208 syllables with hiragana unfinished after
  a month — plus the note that the ceiling had to move with the base or the high-retention bump would
  silently do nothing. Placement, the learner-settable pace, `daily_new_items_target` and the
  nothing-to-do day are all described, since the plan never mentioned any of them.
- **HANDOFF.md** closes the kana-pace open question with the table that answered it, and drops the
  claim that "the code implements the plan verbatim" — no longer true, and the six product-level
  departures are now listed explicitly. Its two "not in PLAN.md" sections said the same thing about
  different kinds of decision, so they are now separated into implementation and product.
- **README.md** describes the pace, practice sittings, placement, free recall and the empty-day rule
  in the lesson walkthrough, none of which existed when it was written.
